content: If necessary, waste materials should be collected using a vacuum pickup system. The collected waste must be placed in sealed containers that are clearly labeled to indicate their contents. Cleanup and disposal procedures must be carried out in a manner that prevents worker contact with the waste and complies with all applicable local, state, and federal regulations. Workers must be provided with facilities for showering and changing clothes at the end of each work shift. Records must include the name of the worker being monitored, their social security number, the duties performed, job locations, dates and times of measurements, sampling and analytical methods used, the type of personal protection employed (if any), and the number, duration, and results of samples taken. Additionally, the physician's written statement, results of medical examinations and tests, medical complaints, and other relevant information must be retained in the medical files of all workers exposed to airborne concentrations of EGBE or EGBEA at or above the action level in the workplace. Copies of applicable environmental monitoring data must also be included in the worker's medical file. In accordance with Section 20 of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, employers must, upon request, allow the subject worker, former worker, or anyone with specific written consent from the subject or former worker to examine and copy exposure monitoring records. Any required medical records must also be made available for examination and copying under the same conditions. This document outlines the criteria and recommended standards necessary to prevent health impairment from exposure to EGBE and EGBEA, two solvents primarily used in surface coatings. Acute overexposure to these compounds can cause irritation of the eyes, nose, and throat, as well as symptoms such as drowsiness, nausea, tremors, and weakness. Chronic or repeated exposure may result in damage to the bone marrow, blood cells, kidneys, and liver. The document was developed in response to Section 20(a)(3) of the Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) Act of 1970, which mandates NIOSH to establish criteria for toxic materials and harmful physical agents to define exposure concentrations that ensure no worker suffers impaired health, functional capacity, or reduced life expectancy due to work experience. NIOSH has formalized a system for developing criteria to establish standards that protect workers exposed to hazardous chemical and physical agents. Compliance with these standards is not the sole objective; the criteria and recommendations are also intended to assist management and labor in developing improved engineering controls and healthier work practices. The recommended standards for EGBE and EGBEA apply exclusively to workplace exposures resulting from the processing, manufacturing, handling, and use of these substances. These recommendations are not designed for the general population, and extrapolation beyond the occupational environment may not be appropriate. The standards aim to protect workers from both acute and chronic effects of EGBE and EGBEA exposure. Exposure concentrations are measurable using valid, reproducible techniques available to industry and government agencies. The document assesses the hazards associated with occupational exposure to EGBE and EGBEA. Chapter 1 presents the recommended standard and its requirements. Chapter 3 provides information on the chemical and physical properties of EGBE and EGBEA, production methods, uses, and the extent of worker exposure. Chapter 4 discusses and summarizes the effects of exposure to these glycol ethers on humans and animals. Subsequent chapters describe environmental sampling and analytical methods, medical monitoring, existing occupational health standards, and correlations between exposure and health effects.
